title: Therapy Assistant: Hand Over a Changed Participation Goal
prompt: You are a new therapy assistant at fictional Harbour Rehabilitation. An adult arriving for a clinician-planned session says, "The plan mentions stairs, but my priority is getting back to my community choir. I do not want to do the planned activity until I understand why." Exercise policy says assistants respect a pause, record the person's own goal, and ask the supervising therapist to discuss any plan change. They do not prescribe or substitute activities. Respond to the person and give a concise handoff. No diagnosis or exercise instruction is needed.
blurb: Listen to a person's participation goal and seek a therapist discussion without improvising treatment.

rubric.label: Capture the person's goal
rubric.description: Separates the person's meaningful activity from the listed task.

anchors.0: Dismisses choir as irrelevant or says the person must comply.
anchors.2: Acknowledges choir and asks what returning would mean to the person.
anchors.4: Records the person's own desired participation and concern about the plan, checks the summary, and avoids assuming what clinical task would achieve it.

rubric.label: Respect the requested pause
rubric.description: Supports choice and uses the supervising therapist for plan decisions.

anchors.0: Substitutes a new exercise or continues the planned activity over the objection.
anchors.2: Pauses and requests a therapist discussion.
anchors.4: Explains the assistant's role plainly, keeps activity changes with the therapist and person, and offers the supplied quiet waiting or rescheduling choice.

rubric.label: Make the disagreement useful to the therapist
rubric.description: Passes a neutral, specific description rather than a compliance label.

anchors.0: Describes the person as unmotivated or omits the goal.
anchors.2: Relays the request for clarification and choir goal.
anchors.4: Separates the written plan, the person's words, what has paused, and the requested conversation; confirms the therapist owns the next step.

reference.scenario: You are a new therapy assistant at fictional Harbour Rehabilitation. An adult arriving for a clinician-planned session says, "The plan mentions stairs, but my priority is getting back to my community choir. I do not want to do the planned activity until I understand why." Exercise policy says assistants respect a pause, record the person's own goal, and ask the supervising therapist to discuss any plan change. They do not prescribe or substitute activities. Respond to the person and give a concise handoff. No diagnosis or exercise instruction is needed.

facts.value: The person wants to attend a weekly rehearsal with friends but has not explained access barriers. Do not invent a mobility, communication, or swallowing impairment.
facts.reveal_when: candidate asks what choir participation involves

facts.value: The supervising therapist can talk in ten minutes. The person may wait in a quiet area or discuss rescheduling with the coordinator.

model_points: Participation goals can be meaningful without the assistant deciding the clinical relationship to a planned task. Ask and reflect instead of inferring treatment needs.
Respect the pause and refer the plan discussion to the supervising therapist; the assistant can support communication and choices within the supplied role.
Use an objective handoff that preserves the person's goal and uncertainty, avoiding labels such as noncompliant.

probes.trigger: candidate acknowledges the goal but starts the planned activity
probes.question: What did the person ask to happen before proceeding?

probes.trigger: candidate offers to help write questions for the therapist
probes.question: How will you ensure the list reflects the person's priorities rather than your explanation?

probes.trigger: candidate initially calls the person noncompliant then revises
probes.question: How would you correct that label in the handoff?

fair_alternatives: The person may prefer to explain directly to the therapist; the assistant can facilitate rather than speak for them.
A short written goal statement or spoken summary is acceptable. No clinical terminology is required.

Assess the work demonstrated here. Accept relevant examples from education, volunteering, caregiving, placements, or paid work; professional vocabulary and employer pedigree are not evidence of a stronger answer.
reference.assessment_limits: Assess person-centered communication and supervised-role boundaries across allied health. Do not assess treatment selection, exercise technique, diagnosis, or professional registration. Unobserved dimensions are not failures. Credit a reasoned correction and distinguish independently demonstrated reasoning from coached assistance. Do not penalize a candidate for an unrevealed conditional fact; credit appropriate requests and conditional plans, and distinguish candidate assumptions from interviewer-supplied evidence.

interviewer_notes: Assess person-centered communication and supervised-role boundaries across allied health. Do not assess treatment selection, exercise technique, diagnosis, or professional registration. Use only the supplied fictional facts and policies; acknowledge unknowns. Ask one triggered probe at a time after the candidate has finished. Accept plain language and accessible written or spoken explanations. Do not score accent, typing speed, confidence, credentials, or experience with a named employer. Credit revisions and record assistance. All participants are fictional adults; no real patient, client, operational, or confidential data is needed. Allow silence for thinking without treating it as failure. In short sessions prioritize the core decision and one material follow-up, leaving room for a correction and wrap-up.

learning_drills.title: Write a person-centered handoff
learning_drills.prompt: Write a four-line handoff distinguishing planned activity, stated goal, requested pause, and next conversation. This is self-guided practice; no model assessment is performed.
checklist: Do not prescribe an alternative activity
